summary: Specifies NETBLT (NETwork BLock Transfer), a transport-level protocol for quickly moving large amounts of data between computers. It is reliable, flow controlled and aims for high throughput over many kinds of networks. It was experimental, not a standard, and some parts were unfinished. It revises RFC 969.

eli5.summary: Instead of carrying a pile of bricks one at a time, you move them in big, checked batches. This protocol sends data in large blocks to go faster.

subtitle: A bulk transfer protocol that sends big buffers at a negotiated rate instead of using small windows.

tldr.problem: Moving a large amount of data over congested, lossy or long-delay (satellite) paths is slow when a protocol waits on small windows and per-packet interactions.
tldr.mechanism: NETBLT moves data in large client buffers, each sent as a series of packets paced by a negotiated burst size and burst rate. The receiver lists missing packets for each buffer and the sender resends only those.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Experimental revision of RFC 969 published for discussion. It does not constitute a standard, parts were still unspecified, and it advises against implementing it.

sections.title: What NETBLT Is For
sections.content:
NETBLT (NETwork BLock Transfer) is a transport-level protocol for the rapid transfer of a large quantity of data between computers. It is reliable and flow controlled, and it aims for maximum throughput over a wide variety of networks. It runs on top of the Internet Protocol (IP) but should work over any similar datagram protocol.

The aim is higher throughput than other protocols offer, by reducing the effect of network congestion, delays over satellite links, and packet loss. Rate control handles congestion, multiple buffering gives high throughput over long-delay satellite channels, and timeout and retransmit algorithms limit the damage from lost packets.

The Status section says the document is published for discussion and comment and does not constitute a standard. Certain parts of the protocol had not yet been specified, so implementation was not advised.
sections.eli5: NETBLT is a way to send a very big file quickly, even over slow, far-away or messy connections.

sections.title: Buffers and Packets
sections.content:
A transfer opens a connection between two clients, the sender and the receiver, moves the data in large aggregates called buffers, and then closes the connection. The client supplies one buffer at a time, so interaction between NETBLT and its client happens per buffer rather than per packet. The maximum transfer length is 2**32 bytes.

All buffers except the last are the same size, and the sending and receiving NETBLT negotiate that size at connection setup. Each buffer is split into DATA packets, also of one negotiated size except for the last. Packets should be as large as possible but not so large that they cause internetwork fragmentation. NETBLT keeps no copy of a buffer for retransmission and recopies data from the client buffer instead.

Because the receiver does not know the transfer size in advance, the last packet of every buffer is sent as an LDATA packet. It is identical to a DATA packet except for its type.
sections.eli5: The file is cut into big boxes, and each box is packed into many small parcels. The last parcel in each box gets a special sticker so the receiver knows the box is full.

sections.title: Rate Control and Multiple Buffering
sections.content:
Window-based flow control tends to give low throughput because windows must stay small and cannot easily be updated. NETBLT instead uses rate control. The sender transmits a burst of packets over a negotiated time interval, then sends another burst, using timers rather than messages from the receiver. The rate has two parts, a burst size and a burst rate, where burst size divided by burst rate equals the average transmission time per packet.

Packet size, buffer size, burst size and burst rate are negotiated at connection setup. The active end proposes values and the passive end may change them only by making them more restrictive. Burst size and burst rate can be renegotiated after each buffer: the receiver offers values in its OK message and the sender may tighten them in a NULL-ACK packet. As guidance, a burst of five to ten packets should keep overhead acceptable on most modern operating systems.

In the simplest transfer the protocol is lock-step: nothing moves between one buffer finishing and confirmation arriving. With multiple buffering the sender can start the next buffer while earlier ones await an OK or RESEND, so packet flow stays essentially continuous.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking after every parcel whether it can send another, the sender hands over a few parcels at an agreed pace. If the road gets crowded, the two sides agree to slow down.

sections.title: Opening, Transferring and Closing
sections.content:
Setup takes two packets. The active end sends OPEN. The passive end answers with RESPONSE to accept or REFUSED to decline. These packets also negotiate the maximum number of buffers sending at once, a flag for whether DATA packet data is checksummed, and each end's death-timeout value. A 32-bit connection unique ID in OPEN must be returned in RESPONSE, which stops a stale response being mistaken for the current one. The active end identifies itself with a 32-bit Internet address and a unique 16-bit port number.

For data, the receiver sends a GO message inside a CONTROL packet when it has a buffer ready. The sender then transmits the buffer as DATA packets followed by an LDATA packet. The receiver answers with RESEND listing missing packets, or with OK once the buffer is complete.

There are three ways to end a connection. After a successful transfer the sender sets a last-buffer flag on the final buffer, waits for OK messages for all buffers and then dallies before closing, so a lost final acknowledgment can be repaired. The receiver may send a DONE packet to let the sender skip the wait. A client may send QUIT, answered by QUITACK, between buffer transmissions. A NETBLT layer that thinks it or its peer is malfunctioning sends ABORT at any time, with no reliability expected.
sections.eli5: First the two sides say hello and agree on the rules. Then the receiver says it is ready for a box, the sender sends it, and the receiver says which parcels are missing or that all is well. At the end they say goodbye, or one can stop early if something seems broken.

sections.title: Timers and Loss Recovery
sections.content:
Several timers keep the transfer from hanging. The receiver sets a control timer whenever it sends a CONTROL packet. Each control message carries a sequence number starting at one, and the sender returns a high-acknowledged-sequence-number so the receiver knows what arrived. If the timer expires, the whole control packet is resent. Its value is based on network round-trip time plus a variance factor. Because unacknowledged messages stay in the packet and are sent again, most control losses on a noisy channel recover automatically. The sender discards duplicates whose sequence numbers are below its high-acknowledged number.

A lost LDATA packet is handled by a data timer per buffer at the receiver. It is based on the time to transfer a buffer (the number of bursts times the burst rate) plus a variance factor. A first, loose value is replaced by a tight value once the first DATA packet arrives. If it expires, the receiver sends a RESEND for all missing packets. A timer that is too short causes needless RESEND packets and serious performance loss.

Each end also runs a death timer, reset on every received packet. When a NETBLT has nothing else to send it emits KEEPALIVE packets, for example at the death timer value divided by four, so the peer does not assume it has died.
sections.eli5: Each side keeps an egg timer. If a message or parcel does not show up before the timer rings, the receiver asks again. If a side goes completely quiet for too long, the other assumes it is gone and hangs up.

sections.title: Packet Types and Formats
sections.content:
NETBLT is carried directly in IP and has been assigned protocol number 30 (decimal). All packets share a common header holding a checksum, version, type, length, and local and foreign ports. Packets are longword-aligned: lengths are multiples of 4 bytes, and string fields end with at least one null byte plus padding.

There are three groups. NULL-ACK, DATA and LDATA travel from sender to receiver and carry the high-acknowledged sequence number. The CONTROL packet travels only from receiver to sender and holds any number of GO, OK or RESEND messages, each with its own sequence number. The remaining packets (OPEN, RESPONSE, REFUSED, QUIT, QUITACK, DONE, KEEPALIVE and ABORT) have their own reliability arrangements or none, and all but DONE can be sent by either end.

The RFC also notes in Planned Enhancements that NETBLT had no algorithm for choosing its rate-control parameters. In the initial tests, the person running the test set them.
sections.eli5: Every message has the same kind of label on the front saying who it is from, who it is for and what kind of message it is. Each kind of message has its own number.
